title: Learning to Code
summary: How code gives a computer exact step-by-step instructions, and how beginners use blocks, loops, conditions, and debugging to build programs and solve problems.
poll: Every student should learn to code at school.

versions.title: Let's Code!
versions.text:
A computer is smart. But it can not think on its own. We must tell it what to do. The words we use are called code.

A computer does just what the code says. It does each step in order. If the order is wrong, the job goes wrong. It can not guess what you mean.

Think of how you make tea. First, you boil the water. Then you add the tea. Then you pour it. Code is a list of steps like that.

Kids can start with blocks. Each block is one step. You snap the blocks in a line. Then a cat on the screen can move and jump!

Some steps must be done a lot. You do not need to type them each time. You can use a loop. A loop does the same step again and again.

Code can have a mistake. A mistake in code is a bug. You look for it. Then you fix it. That is part of the fun.

Code helps us make games, apps, and robots. Would you like to try it?

Think of how you make a cup of tea. First, you boil the water. Next, you put tea in a cup. Then you pour in the hot water. Code is a list of clear steps, just like that.

Many kids start with blocks. Each block is one step. You snap the blocks in a line. Then a cat on the screen can walk, jump, or talk!

Some steps must be done a lot. You do not have to type them each time. You can use a loop. A loop tells the computer to do the same step again and again.

Code can have a mistake. A mistake in code is called a bug. Coders look for the bug and fix it. Good coders make mistakes, too. That is fine.

Code is used to make games, apps, and robots. It helps you learn to solve a big problem one small step at a time.

A computer does just what the code tells it. It follows each step in order. If the steps are in the wrong order, the job goes wrong. A computer can not guess what you mean.

Think about how you make a cup of tea. First, you boil the water. Next, you put tea in a cup. Then you pour in the hot water. Code is a list of clear steps, just like this.

Many kids start with blocks. Each block is one step. You snap the blocks together in a line. Then a cat on the screen can walk, jump, or talk!

Some steps must be done many times. You do not have to write them over and over. You can use a loop. A loop tells the computer to do the same step again and again.

versions.title: Learning to Code
versions.text:
A computer is a very fast machine, but it cannot think for itself. People have to tell it exactly what to do. The instructions we write for a computer are called code.

A computer follows code exactly. It carries out each step in order, one after another. If the steps are in the wrong order, the result will be wrong. A computer cannot guess what you meant to say.

Think about making a cup of tea. First, you boil the water. Next, you put a tea bag in a cup. Then you pour in the hot water. Code works the same way. It is a list of clear steps that solve a problem.

Many young coders begin with blocks. Each block stands for one step. You snap the blocks together, like puzzle pieces. Then a character on the screen can walk, jump, or speak.

Some steps need to happen many times. Instead of writing them again and again, you can use a loop. A loop tells the computer to repeat the same steps.

Sometimes code has a mistake. A mistake in code is called a bug. Coders search for the bug and fix it. Even expert coders make mistakes, so finding bugs is a normal part of the job.

People use code to make games, apps, and robots. Learning to code also teaches you to solve big problems by breaking them into small steps.

versions.title: Learning to Code
versions.text:
A computer is a very fast machine, but it cannot think for itself. People have to tell it exactly what to do. The steps we write for a computer are called code. We write them in a programming language.

A computer follows code just as it is written. It does each step in order, and this order is called a sequence. If the sequence is wrong, the result will be wrong. A computer cannot guess what you meant.

A set of steps that solves a problem is called an algorithm. You use algorithms every day. Making a cup of tea is one. First, boil the water. Next, put a tea bag in a cup. Then pour in the water. Code turns ideas like this into steps a computer can follow.

Many beginners start with a block language called Scratch. Each block is one step, and you snap the blocks together like puzzle pieces. Later, many coders move on to typed languages such as Python.

Code also uses a few big ideas. A loop repeats steps, so you do not have to write them again and again. A condition lets a program make a choice. For example, "If the player touches the wall, then the game is over."

Mistakes in code are called bugs. Fixing them is called debugging. The word has a fun history. In 1947, engineers working with computer scientist Grace Hopper found a real moth stuck inside a computer.

People use code to build games, apps, and robots. Learning it also teaches you to solve big problems one small step at a time.

versions.title: Learning to Code
versions.text:
A computer is an extraordinarily fast machine, yet it cannot think for itself. People must tell it precisely what to do. The instructions we write for a computer are called code, and we write them in a special programming language.

A computer follows code exactly as it is written. It carries out each instruction in order, and this order is called a sequence. If the sequence is incorrect, the result will also be incorrect, because a computer cannot guess what the programmer intended.

A set of steps that solves a problem is called an algorithm. You already use algorithms every day without realizing it. Making a cup of tea is one example: boil the water, place a tea bag in a cup, and then pour in the water. Code transforms everyday ideas like this into precise steps a computer can follow.

Many beginners start with a block-based language such as Scratch, which was developed at a university in the United States. Each block represents one instruction, and you connect the blocks like puzzle pieces. Later, many students move on to typed languages such as Python.

Code also depends on a few powerful ideas. A loop repeats steps, so programmers do not have to write the same instructions again and again. A condition allows a program to make decisions. For example, "If the player touches the wall, then the game is over."

Mistakes in code are called bugs, and locating and correcting them is called debugging. The word has a surprising history. In 1947, engineers working with computer scientist Grace Hopper discovered an actual moth trapped inside a computer.

Today people use code to build games, applications, websites, and robots. Learning to code also trains your mind to solve complicated problems by dividing them into manageable steps.

A computer is an extraordinarily fast machine, yet it cannot think for itself. People must tell it precisely what to do, and the instructions they write are called code. These instructions are written in a programming language, which has its own vocabulary and rules.

A computer follows code exactly as it is written. It carries out each instruction in order, and this order is known as a sequence. If the sequence is incorrect, the result will also be incorrect, because a computer cannot guess what the programmer intended.

A set of steps that solves a problem is called an algorithm. You already use algorithms every day without realizing it. Making a cup of tea is one example: boil the water, place a tea bag in a cup, and then pour in the water. Programming transforms everyday ideas like this into precise steps that a computer can follow.

Many beginners start with a block-based language such as Scratch, which was developed at a university in the United States. Each block represents one instruction, and students connect the blocks like puzzle pieces. Later, many learners move on to typed languages such as Python, which professionals also use.

Code also depends on several powerful ideas. A loop repeats steps, so programmers do not have to write identical instructions again and again. A condition allows a program to make decisions. For example, "If the player touches the wall, then the game is over."

Mistakes in code are called bugs, and locating and correcting them is called debugging. The word has a surprising history. In 1947, engineers working with the computer scientist Grace Hopper discovered an actual moth trapped inside a computer, and they recorded it as a "bug."

Today people use code to build games, applications, websites, and robots. Learning to code also trains your mind to solve complicated problems by dividing them into smaller, manageable steps.

versions.title: Learning to Code
versions.text:
A computer is an extraordinarily fast machine, yet it cannot think independently. People must tell it precisely what to do. The instructions they write are called code, and they are written in a programming language. Each language has its own vocabulary and its own strict rules, which are known as syntax.

A computer follows code exactly as it is written, carrying out each instruction in a particular order called a sequence. If the sequence is incorrect, the result will also be incorrect, because a computer cannot guess what the programmer intended; its logic is completely literal.

A set of steps that solves a problem is called an algorithm. People use algorithms every day without realizing it. Making a cup of tea is one example: you boil the water, place a tea bag in a cup, and then pour in the water. Programming transforms everyday procedures like this into precise instructions that a computer can follow.

Many beginners start with a block-based language such as Scratch, which was developed at a university in the United States. Each block represents one instruction, and the blocks connect like puzzle pieces, so students cannot make spelling mistakes. Later, many learners progress to typed languages such as Python, where the syntax must be exact, since a single missing symbol can stop a program from running.

Code also depends on several powerful ideas. A loop repeats steps, which makes a program shorter and more efficient. A condition allows a program to make decisions, as in "If the player touches the wall, then the game is over."

Mistakes in code are called bugs, and locating and correcting them is called debugging. In 1947, engineers working with the computer scientist Grace Hopper discovered an actual moth trapped inside a computer, and they recorded it as a "bug." Since programs rarely work perfectly the first time, persistence is one of a programmer's most valuable qualities.

Learning to code strengthens problem solving as well, because programmers learn to decompose a large challenge into smaller, manageable parts and solve them one at a time. Schools in many countries, including Saudi Arabia, now teach coding, since these skills are useful in mathematics, science, and many future careers.

versions.title: Learning to Code
versions.text:
A computer is an extraordinarily fast machine, yet it is incapable of thinking independently, so people must tell it precisely what to do. The instructions they compose are called code, and they are written in a programming language that possesses its own specialized vocabulary and its own strict grammatical regulations, which are collectively known as syntax.

A computer follows code exactly as it is written, executing every instruction in a particular order called a sequence. If the sequence is incorrect, the result will inevitably be incorrect as well, because a computer cannot interpret what the programmer intended; its logic is entirely literal.

A set of steps that solves a problem is called an algorithm, and people use algorithms continually without recognizing them. Preparing a cup of tea is one illustration: you boil the water, place a tea bag in a cup, and subsequently pour in the water. Programming transforms everyday procedures like this into unambiguous instructions that a computer can reliably follow.

Many beginners start with a block-based language such as Scratch, which was developed at a university in the United States. Because each block represents a single instruction and the blocks interlock like puzzle pieces, students cannot make spelling or punctuation errors. Afterward, many learners progress to typed languages such as Python, in which the syntax must be absolutely exact, since a single missing symbol can prevent an entire program from operating.

Code also depends on several fundamental concepts. A loop repeats instructions, which makes a program shorter and considerably more efficient, whereas a conditional statement enables a program to make decisions, as in "If the player touches the wall, then the game is over."

Mistakes in code are called bugs, and the methodical process of identifying and correcting them is called debugging. In 1947, engineers collaborating with the computer scientist Grace Hopper discovered an actual moth trapped inside a computer, and they documented it as a "bug." Because programs rarely function perfectly on the initial attempt, persistence is one of a programmer's most valuable characteristics.

Learning to code strengthens general problem-solving abilities as well, because programmers learn to decompose an intimidating challenge into smaller, manageable components and resolve them systematically. Educational systems in numerous countries, including Saudi Arabia, now incorporate coding into their curricula, since these abilities are valuable in mathematics, science, and a remarkable variety of future occupations.

keyWords.example: Please line up in order from the shortest to the tallest.

keyWords.definition: a piece you can put together with other pieces
keyWords.example: The little boy stacked one block on top of another.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to fix a broken computer screen
How people use code to tell computers what to do
Why cats like to play games on a computer screen
How to make the best cup of tea
questions.why: The whole article explains code: steps in order, blocks, loops, and bugs.

wrong.A: The article is not about fixing screens.
wrong.C: A cat appears on the screen in a block program, but cats are not the topic.
wrong.D: Tea is only an example of steps.

questions.stem: What does a computer do with code?
options: It does just what the code says, step by step.
It guesses what you mean and changes the steps.
It skips the steps it does not like.
It writes new code all by itself.
questions.why: The article says a computer does just what the code says and does each step in order.

wrong.B: The article says a computer can not guess what you mean.
wrong.C: A computer follows every step; it does not skip steps.
wrong.D: People must tell the computer what to do.

questions.stem: In the article, what does a loop do?
options: It turns the computer off when the job is done.
It finds a mistake in the code.
It does the same step again and again.
It snaps two blocks apart.
questions.why: The article says a loop tells the computer to do the same step again and again.

wrong.A: A loop does not turn off the computer.
wrong.B: Finding mistakes is fixing a bug, not a loop.
wrong.D: A loop repeats steps; it does not take blocks apart.

questions.stem: What is a bug in code?
options: A small insect on the keyboard
A block that makes a cat jump
A list of steps for making tea
A mistake in the code
questions.why: The article says a mistake in code is called a bug.

wrong.A: In this article, a bug is a mistake, not an insect.
wrong.C: The tea steps are an example of code, not a bug.

questions.stem: What happens if the steps in code are in the wrong order?
options: The computer fixes the order for you.
The job goes wrong.
The code runs faster.
The blocks change color.
questions.why: The article says that if the order is wrong, the job goes wrong.

wrong.A: A computer can not guess what you mean, so it does not fix the order.
wrong.C: The article does not say wrong order makes code faster.
wrong.D: The article does not mention blocks changing color.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell how to make tea?

To teach readers how to make a new kind of hot drink
To tell where tea comes from

wrong.B: The tea steps are an example, not a recipe lesson.
wrong.C: The article does not say where tea comes from.
wrong.D: The article never says computers make tea.
